Paul. Originally Saul of Tarsus, a persecutor of early Christians who underwent a dramatic conversion on the road to Damascus after encountering the risen Jesus. Before his conversion, he persecuted Christians, overseeing the execution of Stephen and jailing believers. His transformative vision on the road to Damascus, encountering the risen Jesus and hearing his voice, redirected his entire life. He was renamed Paul as a symbol of his new mission and traveled throughout the Mediterranean world as an apostle. He preached to Gentiles and argued that salvation through Jesus was available to all peoples, not just Jews. He authored thirteen epistles addressing theology, church practice, and spiritual instruction, writing more than half of all New Testament epistles. He suffered imprisonments, beatings, and shipwrecks in service of his mission, enduring persecution he once inflicted on others. He debated with Peter at Antioch over the inclusion of Gentiles, a crucial moment in early Christian theology. Traditional accounts describe his martyrdom by beheading in Rome, where he had been imprisoned.
